CRAFT: Coaching Reinforcement Learning Autonomously using Foundation Models for Multi-Robot Coordination Tasks

Seoyeon Choi    Kanghyun Ryu    Jonghoon Ock Affiliation: Seoyeon Choi, Kanghyun Ryu, Jonghoon Ock, and Negar Mehr is with Mechanical Engineering, University of California Berkeley {seoyeon99, kanghyun.ryu, ockjh228, negar}@berkeley.edu    Negar Mehr ††thanks: *Equal contribution Affiliation: Seoyeon Choi, Kanghyun Ryu, Jonghoon Ock, and Negar Mehr is with Mechanical Engineering, University of California Berkeley {seoyeon99, kanghyun.ryu, ockjh228, negar}@berkeley.edu
Abstract

Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) provides a powerful framework for learning coordination in multi-agent systems. However, applying MARL to robotics still remains challenging due to high-dimensional continuous joint action spaces, complex reward design, and non-stationary transitions inherent to decentralized settings. On the other hand, humans learn complex coordination through staged curricula, where long-horizon behaviors are progressively built upon simpler skills. Motivated by this, we propose CRAFT: Coaching Reinforcement learning Autonomously using Foundation models for multi-robot coordination Tasks, a framework that leverages the reasoning capabilities of foundation models to act as a “coach” for multi-robot coordination. CRAFT automatically decomposes long-horizon coordination tasks into sequences of subtasks using the planning capability of Large Language Models (LLMs). In what follows, CRAFT trains each subtask using reward functions generated by LLM, and refines them through a Vision Language Model (VLM)-guided reward-refinement loop. We evaluate CRAFT on multi-quadruped navigation and bimanual manipulation tasks, demonstrating its capability to learn complex coordination behaviors. In addition, we validate the multi-quadruped navigation policy in real hardware experiments.

I Introduction

Learning coordinated behaviors is essential for enabling robots to work together in real-world tasks, yet achieving such coordination remains a significant challenge. Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) offers a promising framework, with notable successes in domains such as real-time strategy games [1, 2] and simulated sports [3], and it is increasingly being explored for multi-robot coordination [4, 5]. However, applying MARL to robotics is notoriously difficult due to the high-dimensional action spaces and sparse rewards inherent in robotic tasks alongside the non-stationarity introduced by decentralized decision-making. To coordinate effectively, robots need to reason about each other’s actions and navigate complex credit assignment problems [6]. These challenges become even more pronounced in multi-robot domains that involve physical interaction, long-horizon planning, and intricate cooperation. In this paper, we consider the problem of teaching robots to coordinate with one another by developing an automatic curriculum generation and learning pipeline that enables MARL policies to acquire effective coordination strategies in complex multi-robot tasks.

In the physical world, humans learn complex coordination progressively. For example, a soccer team begins with simple cooperative drills, such as short passes, before advancing to elaborate team strategies. As such, curriculum generation has been studied as an effective approach for learning coordination and strategies in MARL domains by structuring the training into stages of increasing complexity [7]. A curriculum breaks a complex task into a sequence of subtasks where early subtasks help agents learn fundamental skills. As training progresses, long-horizon objectives are decomposed into manageable subtasks that build on these fundamentals, allowing agents to gradually master complicated coordination strategies. Through this staged progression, curriculum generation enables the emergence of complex long-horizon collaborative behaviors that are difficult to achieve when training agents directly on the target task [5, 8, 9].

Despite its effectiveness, curriculum design is often nontrivial as it requires domain knowledge to identify key steps in long-horizon tasks and reasoning ability to monitor the learning progress [10]. Meanwhile, recent advances in foundation models, such as Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs), have introduced human-like reasoning capabilities to robot learning. These reasoning capabilities have been leveraged for task decomposition [11, 12], reward shaping [13, 14], and policy evaluation [15, 16]. We argue, however, that these models can go beyond such individual applications and instead serve as a coach, i.e. entity that teaches agents how to coordinate. Coaching naturally integrates all these skills: a good coach breaks down the task, defines success criteria for each subtask, and provides actionable feedback to guide improvement.

In this paper, we introduce CRAFT: Coaching Reinforcement learning Autonomously using Foundation models for multi-robot coordination Tasks. CRAFT first decomposes a complex cooperative task into sequences of subtasks that facilitate the learning of intricate multi-agent coordination policies. Then, each subtask is paired with an LLM-generated reward function in executable code, while a VLM provides feedback on trained policies to iteratively refine rewards through a VLM-guided reward-refinement loop. Through this process, CRAFT produces curricula for long-horizon coordination tasks, designs semantically rich reward functions, and evaluates task–policy alignment using visual information. Through experiments in simulation and on physical robots, we demonstrate that CRAFT enables learning coordination behaviors in multi-quadruped navigation and bimanual manipulation tasks that standard learning methods fail to solve.

In summary, our contributions are the following:

  1. 1.

    We propose CRAFT, a framework that automatically designs curricula for long-horizon multi-robot coordination tasks by leveraging the reasoning capabilities of foundation models.

  2. 2.

    We evaluate CRAFT on multi-quadruped navigation and bimanual manipulation tasks, which require long-horizon coordination. CRAFT learns complex coordination policies that were infeasible without human-designed curricula or hand-calibrated rewards.

  3. 3.

    We validate the multi-quadruped navigation policies learned with CRAFT in hardware experiments, demonstrating their real-world transferability.

II Related Works

II-A Curriculum Learning and Foundation Models

Curriculum learning accelerates RL by structuring training as a sequence of subtasks with increasing difficulty [8]. It has been shown to improve sample efficiency [17], enable the learning of challenging tasks [8], and support multitask learning [18]. While many prior works on curriculum design have relied on trial-and-error of human experts [9, 19], more recent efforts have explored leveraging the reasoning capabilities of LLMs for automated curriculum design [20, 21, 22]. In this work, we extend curricula design with foundation models to multi-agent settings, where reasoning about agent interactions and long-horizon task decomposition is even more critical.

II-B LLM/VLM for Reward Design

Recent works have shown the effectiveness of reasoning and general knowledge of foundation models for reward design. Several works leverage language models to generate reward functions in executable code and further refine them through evolutionary search [13, 23]. Others use VLM’s ability to evaluate alignment between visual observations and language descriptions, directly querying a VLM for the reward [14] or providing other feedback to the policy, such as success or failure [15, 16, 24]. Building on these works, we employ the reward generation capabilities of LLMs to produce reward functions for each subtask in a curriculum, and use a VLM to evaluate trained policies and provide feedback for refining reward functions.

II-C Multi-robot Coordination

Several works have explored MARL for multi-robot coordination. For a team of quadrupeds, MARL has been employed in hierarchical structure where it learns high-level coordination behavior for object manipulation [25, 26] or soccer [4], combined with low-level locomotion policy. However, these methods rely on either carefully designed reward functions [25] or manually specified curricula [26]. MARL also has been used for multi-robot navigation with collision avoidance in aerial [27] or mobile robots [28]. Notably, curriculum learning frameworks have been actively employed in MARL training [4, 26, 27], demonstrating their effectiveness in learning complex coordination behaviors. Based on these successful curriculum learning experiences in MARL, our aim is to automate curriculum design using foundation models, thereby enabling learning complex coordination behaviors while reducing the need for extensive human intervention in MARL.

III Problem Formulation

In this work, we aim to learn a multi-agent coordination problem where a team of agents learn how to coordinate to achieve a target task ℳt​a​r​g​e​t\mathcal{M}_{target}. We model the target task as a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process (Dec-POMDP [29]), defined by the tuple ℳt​a​r​g​e​t=⟨N,𝒮,𝒜,O,P,Rt​a​r​g​e​t,γ⟩\mathcal{M}_{target}=\langle N,\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},O,P,R_{target},\gamma\rangle, where NN is the number of agents, 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the global state space, and 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the joint action space of the agents. We denote the local observation of each agent ii at the global state ss as oi=O⁡(s,i)o^{i}=O(s;i). The joint action of all NN agents is denoted as a=(a1,…,aN)a=(a^{1},\dots,a^{N}), where aia^{i} is the action of agent ii. The transition probability from state ss to s′s^{\prime} when taking the joint action aa is denoted as P⁡(s′|s,a)P(s^{\prime}|s,a). We assume that there exists a shared reward function Rt​a​r​g​e​t​(s,a,s′)R_{target}(s,a,s^{\prime}) that agents need to collectively optimize, and γ\gamma is the discount factor. In this work, we train a MARL policy using a centralized training and decentralized execution (CTDE) framework [29, 30], where all agents share the same policy πθ​(ai|oi)\pi_{\theta}(a^{i}|o^{i}) that observes each agent’s local observation oio^{i} and outputs its action aia^{i}. Our goal is to learn the shared policy πθ​(ai|oi)\pi_{\theta}(a^{i}|o^{i}) such that it maximizes the expected discounted reward J⁡(θ)=𝔼at,st​[∑t∞γt​Rt​a​r​g​e​t​(st,at,st+1)]J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{a_{t},s_{t}}\left[\sum_{t}^{\infty}{\gamma^{t}R_{target}(s_{t},a_{t},s_{t+1})}\right].

We define a curriculum 𝒞\mathcal{C} as a sequence of KK subtasks 𝒞=[ℳ1,ℳ2,…,ℳK]\mathcal{C}=[\mathcal{M}_{1},\mathcal{M}_{2},\dots,\mathcal{M}_{K}], where ℳk\mathcal{M}_{k} denotes the kk-th subtask. Each subtask ℳk\mathcal{M}_{k} is constructed by replacing the reward Rt​a​r​g​e​tR_{target} in ℳt​a​r​g​e​t\mathcal{M}_{target} to its own unique reward RkR_{k}. Then, a curriculum can equivalently be described as a sequence of reward functions [R1,R2,…,RK]\left[R_{1},R_{2},\dots,R_{K}\right]. Therefore, we aim to optimize a sequence of reward functions [R1,R2,…,RK]\left[R_{1},R_{2},\dots,R_{K}\right] so that the final learned policy can accomplish ℳt​a​r​g​e​t\mathcal{M}_{target}.

IV Method

Motivated by how human coaches train teams for coordination tasks, our method leverages LLMs and VLMs as a coach for teaching robots on how to coordinate. In training a team for complex coordination, a coach would first decompose the target task into a sequence of subtasks that specify the details of the coordination strategy. The coach then trains the team on each subtask by defining its objectives (rewards). Once training is complete, the coach evaluates the team’s performance, deciding whether to progress to the next subtask or revisit the current one. Inspired by this process, our framework follows five key stages as shown in Fig. :

  1. 1.

    Curriculum generation module – A curriculum LLM decomposes the long-horizon coordination task into a sequence of subtasks described in natural language.

  2. 2.

    Reward function generation module – A reward generation LLM generates a reward function in executable python code based on the natural language descriptions of the subtasks, providing dense rewards that clearly specify the desired behavior for each subtask.

  3. 3.

    Policy evaluation module – An evaluation VLM evaluates the success or failure of the policy trained with the LLM-generated reward based on the visual and quantitative rollouts of the policy.

  4. 4.

    Reward refinement module – If the policy fails to achieve the desired behavior, an advice VLM provides advice on how to change the reward based on the rollout information and learning curve. Then, an LLM takes the advice and refines the reward function.

  5. 5.

    Sequential training of subtasks – Throughout the training, we initialize each subtask with the policy learned from the previous one while motivating exploration to learn the new subtask.

In the following, we discuss each of these modules in detail.

IV-A Curriculum Generation Module

As a first step, we break down a coordination task into a sequence of subtasks. Given a natural language description of the target task and environment, a curriculum LLM outputs a sequence of subtasks in natural language. However, relying solely on zero-shot curriculum generation can result in unstable outputs due to the stochastic nature of LLM responses, ranging from overly simple to unnecessarily long or misaligned with the target task. To mitigate this, we first generate multiple candidate curricula 𝒞i,i∈{1,2,…,I}\mathcal{C}^{i},i\in\{1,2,\dots,I\}. We then prompt the LLM with the environment description, the target task ℳt​a​r​g​e​t\mathcal{M}_{target}, and the candidate curricula, asking it to refine these candidates into a more coherent and effective curriculum. An example is shown in Fig. 2.

Through this process, we obtain the final curriculum 𝒞=[l1,…,lK]\mathcal{C}=[l_{1},...,l_{K}], where lkl_{k} is a natural language description of each subtask ℳk\mathcal{M}_{k}. The description lkl_{k} is grounded in the state variables of the environment to improve reward design and VLM evaluation. For example, in Task 1: Approach Handles (Fig. 2), instead of a vague description such as “each robot arm should get closer to its handle,” the LLM-generated subtask explicitly uses the state variable Euclidean distance to its respective handle, producing the description “each arm minimizes its Euclidean distance to its target handle.”

IV-B Reward Function Generation Module

Based on natural language description lkl_{k}, we generate a subtask-specific reward RkR_{k} for subtask ℳk\mathcal{M}_{k} in executable code. Compared to describing the curriculum through environment configurations [21] or PDDL [31], specifying the task as a reward provides greater flexibility in representing diverse subtasks across different domains. Furthermore, translating the reward into executable code enables seamless integration with existing environments and algorithms. In this subsection, we describe the generation of the initial base reward Rk0R^{0}_{k}. Here, the superscript denotes the refinement index, where Rk0R^{0}_{k} is the base reward for subtask k, while RkjR^{j}_{k} denote the reward obtained after the jj-th refinement that will be discussed in Section IV-D.

To generate a base reward function Rk0R^{0}_{k}, we prompt the LLM with the language description of the environment, current subtask description lkl_{k}, and an example reward function. Since writing reward functions from scratch for high-dimensional multi-agent systems can be challenging, we provide example reward functions, which are simple, structured variations of the environment-provided rewards, along with helper functions for state processing. For instance, in the bimanual manipulation task shown in Fig. 3, a helper function self._get_tilt_degree_cosine() is provided to compute the cosine value of the pot’s tilt angle. Since curriculum learning should exploit knowledge acquired in previous subtasks, we also include the reward functions from earlier subtasks as additional context in the prompt.

When writing a reward function, we prompt the LLM to separate the reward into reward components (e.g. lift_ reward, balance_reward in Fig. 3) during training time. These logs will later be provided as reward component learning curves for reward refinements in Section IV-D. After reward generation, we train a policy πk0\pi_{k}^{0} with the base reward function Rk0R_{k}^{0} via MARL, such as MAPPO [29]. We note that as we assume using CTDE MARL framework, we are designing a reward for a team, rather than specific agents.

IV-C Policy Evaluation Module

Designing an effective reward function from natural language description is challenging, and one-shot LLM-generated rewards often fail to produce the desired behavior. Therefore, we need a verification step to evaluate the trained policy πk0\pi^{0}_{k} and determine whether to advance to the next subtask or retry the current one.

When evaluating a robot policy, humans rely on visual trajectory rollouts to analyze the collaboration between robots and the progress in the subtask. Motivated by this, we use VLMs for evaluating the success or failure of πk0\pi_{k}^{0} by providing a sequence of snapshot images. Moreover, we also provide state variable trajectory data to make it easier for VLMs to conclude the subtask success. This design choice allows our method to be easily applied to various multi-robot platforms and arbitrary LLM-designed subtasks.

However, even state-of-the-art LLMs and VLMs lack a native understanding of 3D motion [32, 33]. This limitation is particularly pronounced in multi-robot environments, where the dimensionality of the state space scales with the number of agents, making it difficult for VLMs to reason about coordination behaviors directly from raw 3D state variables. Therefore, we extract and provide task-relevant metrics, such as Frobenius norm for orientation differences or distance between objects that are easier for LLMs/VLMs to interpret. When the VLM judges the policy to be successful, we proceed to the next subtask ℳk+1\mathcal{M}_{k+1}. If it concludes the policy as a failure, policy evaluation VLM provides failure reasons which are used for refining the current reward function Rk0R_{k}^{0} to be more aligned with the desired behavior.

IV-D Reward Refinement Module

When generated reward Rk0R_{k}^{0} fails to induce the desired behavior, we should design a new reward function and retry the training process. A naive approach to this reward refinement is resampling from the reward generation module with the same prompt [20], or with minimal additional information, such as appending the previously attempted reward function [34]. However, such naive resampling methods require extensive trial and error and are not scalable to high-dimensional multi-agent systems. To overcome this, we draw inspiration from prior works that have suggested that a team of specialized models can be more effective than a single model for complex tasks [35, 36]. Following this, we introduce two additional models: an advice VLM and a refine LLM, which together enable more meaningful refinement.

First, we prompt the advice VLM to generate unrestricted, free-form advice on how to refine the current reward function based on the current subtask description lkl_{k}, the previously attempted reward function RkjR_{k}^{j}, and the failure reason obtained from policy evaluation module in Section IV-C. In addition, we provide the learning curves of individual per-step reward components, which indicate how each component evolved during training. Since these values often oscillate and are difficult to represent as long numerical sequences in text, we instead convert them into graphical images, offering the VLM a compact and interpretable representation.

Second, in the refine LLM, we provide the previously attempted reward function RkjR_{k}^{j} and advice generated by the VLM. The refine LLM then produces a new refined reward Rkj+1R_{k}^{j+1}. Once a new refined reward Rkj+1R^{j+1}_{k} is generated, we train a corresponding policy πkj+1\pi^{j+1}_{k} and iterate through the VLM-guided reward–refinement loop. We allow a maximum of JJ refinement iterations. If the policy still fails after JJ iterations, the LLM selects the best policy among πk0,…,πkJ\pi_{k}^{0},...,\pi_{k}^{J} using rollout information and proceeds to the next subtask. In our experiments, we found that J=3J=3 iterations were sufficient to generate a successful reward. An example of this refinement process is shown in Fig. 3.

IV-E Sequential Training of Subtasks

When moving from one subtask to the next, the challenge lies in balancing exploitation and exploration: the policy should retain useful behaviors learned in the previous subtask, while adapting to the new reward function. To exploit prior knowledge, we initialize the weights of policy πk+1\pi_{k+1} for subtask ℳk+1\mathcal{M}_{k+1} with the weights of policy πk\pi_{k} from subtask ℳk\mathcal{M}_{k}. The initialized policy πk+1\pi_{k+1} is then trained with the reward function Rk+1R_{k+1}. However, because the reward generation LLM is provided with the history of rewards, parts of Rk+1R_{k+1} often resemble RkR_{k}. This can cause a loss of plasticity [37, 38] leading the policy πk+1\pi_{k+1} to converge to a local optimum similar to policy πk\pi_{k}, preventing further learning under the new reward function Rk+1R_{k+1}.

To avoid loss of plasticity and encourage progress on the new subtask, we employ two techniques. First, we reset the exploration parameter of the policy network to reintroduce exploration at the beginning of each subtask training. In our case, we reset the policy standard deviation layer of MAPPO at the beginning of subtask training. This helps the policy to explore other actions while maintaining current behavior and escape the local-optima of the earlier reward function. Furthermore, we reset the value network with random weights [26]. By resetting only the value network while maintaining the actor network weights, the actor can exploit the previous policy while the critic is reinitialized to estimate the value under the new reward function.

V Experiments

In this section, we evaluate our framework in collaborative multi-robot scenarios. We consider a bimanual manipulation task and multi-quadruped navigation tasks that require complex long-horizon coordination. We show that CRAFT can learn coordination that is challenging to achieve with vanilla MARL even with human-designed reward functions. We also validate our quadruped navigation task in hardware to show our policy transfers to real-world.

V-A Experiment Setup

V-A1 Simulation Environments

We evaluate CRAFT in the following multi-agent coordination environments. The environments are shown in Fig. 4.

  • •

    Quadruped Gate: Two quadrupeds should coordinate to pass the narrow gate without collision [39]. We define a task as success when both agents have passed the gate. Each quadruped has a continuous action space of xx- and yy-axis velocities, and yaw velocity.

  • •

    Quadruped Seesaw: Two quadrupeds should coordinate on the seesaw so that one agent climbs up to the platform at the top of the seesaw while the other balances it [39]. We define a task as success when one of the agents reaches the target platform. The action space is identical to Gate environment.

  • •

    Two Arm Lift: Two robot arms should coordinate in lifting the pot together while keeping the pot level [40]. We define a task as success when the pot is lifted above 0.1m and no more tilted than 30 degrees. Each arm has a continuous action space, which consists of six end-effector delta pose, position and orientation changes relative to the current pose, and one gripper state.

These environments are exceptionally challenging for MARL as they demand long-horizon coordination and decentralized control under partial observability. To our knowledge, no prior RL methods without expert demonstrations have succeeded in solving them reliably. We use MAPPO [29], which employs decentralized execution with only local observations, to evaluate CRAFT’s ability to learn decentralized coordination. MAPPO is implemented with OpenRL library [41] for the multi-quadruped navigation, and skrl library [42] for the bimanual manipulation task. We utilize gpt-4o-2024-08-06 as our LLM models and o4-mini-2025-04-16 as our VLM models.

V-A2 Baselines & Ablation Study

We design our experiments such that we answer the following questions.

  1. Q1

    Can our framework learn MARL policies that require complex coordination between multiple robots?

  2. Q2

    Is curriculum learning framework necessary for learning effective coordination policies?

  3. Q3

    To what extent is the reward refinement module necessary for learning successful policies?

To answer Q1, we compare CRAFT with env_reward and example_reward baselines where env_reward uses the environment-provided reward, while example_reward uses the example reward provided to reward generation module of CRAFT. Both baselines are trained without any staged curricula. To answer Q2, we compare CRAFT with no_curriculum, where we use the final reward functions generated by CRAFT that achieved top-three highest success rate. However, we train the policy without a curriculum and fix the reward function during training. This comparison tests whether a well-designed reward function alone is sufficient for successful policy training, or whether staged curriculum is also necessary. Finally, for Q3, we compare CRAFT with a no_refinement baseline, which removes the VLM-guided reward refinement module (Section IV-D). Instead, no_refinement resamples new reward functions from the reward module, relying on the stochasticity of the LLM to generate effective reward functions. To evaluate the consistency of generated curricula and reward functions, we report the effective curricula ratio. In our experiments, many trials collapse to zero success when the curriculum is poorly structured. Therefore, we define effective curricula as curricula that achieves any nonzero success rate.

V-B Simulation Results

Q1: CRAFT can learn successful coordination policies. We provide the success rate curves for policies with top three success rates among 55 experiments in Fig. 6. In all three environments, CRAFT achieves the highest success rate. We emphasize that CRAFT achieves successful policies without expert demonstrations or hand-crafted curricula, reaching maximum success rates of up to 90% in Quadruped Gate, 60% in Quadruped Seesaw, and 100% in Two Arm Lift. In contrast, env_reward achieves a 0% success rate in most experiments, despite having a dense reward function designed by the environment developers. These results underscore both the difficulty of the benchmarks and the effectiveness of our framework. In addition, while example_reward that was provided to CRAFT also shows less than 10%10\% success rate in every environments, CRAFT designs effective curricula from it and achieves much higher success rate. This demonstrates that curriculum training and reward searching process of CRAFT enables learning a coordination policy that was challenging for vanilla MARL training. The performance gap is especially evident in the Two Arm Lift task, which requires both long-horizon planning and control over high-dimensional action spaces, highlighting the strength of CRAFT in complex multi-robot settings.

Qualitatively, we observe that policies trained with env_reward and example_reward are susceptible to falling into local optima, resulting in suboptimal behaviors. As shown in Fig. 5, a policy trained with env_reward converges to suboptimal strategies, such as grasping the pot but failing to lift it. This arises because long-horizon tasks require a mixture of multiple reward components for different subtasks, such as reaching the pot, grasping, and lifting it. In such cases, it is difficult to design a reward whose global optimum aligns with the desired behavior. Furthermore, even with a well-designed reward function, the presence of multiple local optima can still lead to suboptimal policies.

Q2: Sequential training with curriculum can achieve success rate beyond vanilla training, though its impact varies by task. Following up to Q1, we aim to answer whether a good reward function alone is sufficient for long-horizon coordination, or whether sequential training of the curriculum is also necessary. Overall, CRAFT achieves higher success rates than no_curriculum across all three environments. The gap is especially large in Quadruped Gate and Two Arm Lift, where staged training yields policies with success rates that no_curriculum cannot match even with the same reward functions. In Quadruped Seesaw, no_curriculum achieves a comparable success rate to CRAFT, but we note that it benefits from the well-designed reward function produced by CRAFT. By contrast, env_reward and example_reward fail to learn effective coordination in any environment, underscoring the role of CRAFT’s reward-refinement loop in producing well-shaped rewards that extend beyond those provided by the environment.

Q3: The VLM-guided reward-refinement loop in CRAFT improves curricula reliability. We report the effective curricula ratio and maximum success rate from multiple runs in Table I. With the VLM-guided reward-refinement, CRAFT achieves higher effective curricula ratio than the no_refinement baseline. This highlights that VLM-guided reward-refinement loop contributes to reliable subtask training, leading to consistent generation of effective curricula and corresponding reward functions. We note that if no_refinement generates successful curricula, it also learns a comparable policy, as demonstrated in the maximum success rate in Table I. However, its unreliable curriculum generation strongly degrades its average performance shown in Fig. 6.

V-C Hardware Validation

We validate our method by transferring the learned policy to real robots on the Quadruped Gate task. The policy is first trained in simulation using CRAFT and then deployed on hardware. We use one Unitree Go2 and one Unitree Go1 robot. Since the embodiments and low-level MPC controllers differ from in simulation, we applied action component-wise scaling to the policy outputs before deployment.

As shown in Fig.  and Fig. 7, our method successfully transfers to the real world. The two quadrupeds exhibit coordinated behavior: the blue robot passes through the gate first while the orange robot waits, then proceeds once the gate is clear. Without any additional fine-tuning, our zero-shot transferred policy achieves a success rate of over 60%, serving as a solid baseline given that no further learning is performed after simulation training.

VI Conclusions

In this paper, we proposed CRAFT, a framework to train long-horizon multi-robot coordination tasks. We leveraged the reasoning capabilities of foundation models, with LLMs and VLMs acting as a “coach” to decompose complex behaviors into curricula of subtasks, each paired with an LLM-generated reward function. A VLM-guided reward-refinement loop further improves these rewards, producing semantically rich reward signals that enable successful learning in long-horizon coordination tasks. Through our experiments in multi-quadruped navigation and bimanual manipulation, we demonstrated that our method is effective and also transferable to real hardware.

A key limitation of CRAFT is the variability across trials, as the stochasticity of foundation models can cause occasional failures. However, this variability is not a major obstacle, since we can run multiple training attempts in simulation and deploy only successful policies in real-world. We also view this stochasticity as an advantage since diverse curricula and refinements often yield more creative and effective solutions. Future work can focus on improving reliability in the trials and balancing creativity with stability in foundation-model-driven robot learning.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.
